title: Finally adding recursive functions to Futhark
excerpt: A high-performance and high-level purely functional data-parallel array programming language that can execute on the GPU and CPU.
content_html:
Posted on August 5, 2026

Futhark is unusual among functional languages by not currently supporting recursive functions. This is not because we think recursion is inherently bad - the Futhark compiler itself contains plenty of recursive definitions. The reason is that until recently, we did not have a good answer for how to compile recursive functions in all positions on every backend, and in Futhark we prefer making only promises we can keep. This post will explain why recursion has been a touchy subject for all of Futhark’s existence, why we think we can finally address it, some unexpected trouble that arose when I thought it would be easy, and why Futhark programmers still may want to not use it much.

I considered titling this blog post “restoring recursion to Futhark”, since technically the very earliest drafts of Futhark did support recursive functions until they were removed in 2017. That means we have been without them for most of Futhark’s lifetime, and particularly during the era where Futhark grew into a proper usable language with features like modules, higher-order functions, and size types. Further, they never worked all that well, and would crash the compiler if you used recursion in the wrong place.

The trouble with recursion

The reason we do not currently have recursive functions is fairly simple: they do not work well in GPU kernels, for multiple reasons. The most immediate one is that GPU threads necessarily have tiny stacks. Another reason is that it is also impractical (or slow, or impossible) to allocate memory from within GPU code, meaning all memory has to be pre-allocated in advance - this is difficult when you have a recursive function, where the total memory requirements depends on dynamic control flow decisions. Plain sequential loops are simpler, because once a loop iteration is done, you never return to it - but for (non-tail) recursive functions, you have to keep the activation record intact for an unbounded period of time.

It is not difficult to imagine a rule that says “you can have recursive functions, but not in code that ends up running on a GPU”. What is more difficult is precisely specifying such a rule. Futhark is not a “GPU language”, but rather a hardware-agnostic data parallel language, and we do not want to complicate the type system to track whether a function contains recursion. Futhark has several compiler backends that target CPUs, and for those recursion is straightforward to implement, but the possibility of compiling a program for a GPU means that language restrictions are composed of the union of the restrictions of all supported compiler targets.

This is because the overarching dream of my own research is that if you have a function f, then I want to be able to map that function f efficiently over a collection xs, no matter the size of the collection xs, what f might do, or what machine this is running on. Since people keep coming up with new machines and new fs, I will probably spend my entire career on this, but I digress. My point is that I would not be satisfied with a solution that is complicated or lacks orthogonality, and I don’t want functions that cannot be mapped.

It turned out that lack of recursion is not that big a deal in a functional array language like Futhark. Since the core datatype (arrays) is not inductive, there is not that much to recurse over, and Futhark provides loop syntax for expressing certain kinds of tail recursion (although we do not plan to support actual tail call optimisation for reasons previously explained).

Still, there are some cases where recursion is the natural way to solve problems, mainly recursive divide-and-conquer. Many of the algorithms in A Library of Parallel Algorithms are quite awkward to express in Futhark, and require manual transformation and flattening (but do run fairly fast once that is done). It sure would be nice if we would write code as nice as what Guy Blelloch did in NESL.

Handling recursion with flattening

There are many special cases of recursion that can be handled in various efficient ways (tail recursion is one), but before we can get to that, we need a general solution for all cases, even if that general solution will in the future merely be a fallback solution. Our general solution (which is only necessary when using a GPU backend, remember) comes from flattening. When flattening an expression map f xs where f contains recursion, the recursion is effectively “interchanged” with the map, meaning the recursion ends up outside of all parallel code sections. From an operational perspective, after flattening all recursive control flow is executed on the CPU, while the GPU performs fully flat parallel operations. To give an intuition for how flattening works in this case, suppose we have the hello world of recursive functional programming:

def fact n = if n == 0 then 1 else n * fact (n-1)

And now suppose we are mapping this function over an array of integers:

map fact ns

Obviously this is not a useful thing to do, but it serves as a simple example. Among various boilerplate, flattening will produce a lifted form of fact that is as recursive as the original fact, but operates on an array ns instead of a single n. This lifted function simulates a “single iteration” of the recursion, and then performs a recursive call with those elements of ns that have not yet reached their base case. Simplifying the book-keeping and notation and adding explanatory names, it looks like this:

def fact_lifted ns =
  let (ns_zero, ns_nonzero) = partition_inputs ns
  let ns_nonzero' = map2 (*) ns_nonzero (fact_lifted ns_nonzero)
  let result = combine_inputs (map (const 1) ns_zero) ns_nonzero'
  in result

As in the flattening post, I’m mostly hand-waving how combine_inputs manages to put things together in the right order. The key property is that fact_lifted is only ever invoked from the CPU. Of course, while this works, it is in many cases horrendously slow - both partition_inputs and combine_inputs hide a lot of data movement, but in the near term, general correctness is all we care about - performance can come later.

I thought that once we had an implementation of full flattening, recursion would be easy to add. Of course, nine years of intensive development of the compiler meant that many parts assumed non-recursive programs, and had to be repaired. Most of these changes were not very interesting, but a few uncovered issues that I had not predicted.

Handling recursion in the type checker

Futhark’s type checker was recently largely rewritten, and proper support for recursion was part of the motivation. Since our type checking algorithm is basically conventional Hindley-Milner, supporting recursion was straightforward, although I had a moment where I realised that I actually didn’t know how to do it, because all my Hindley-Milner implementation experience was for nonrecursive languages.

Similarly to Standard ML, but unlike Haskell, Futhark does not support polymorphic recursion - any recursive call must instantiate the recursive function with the same type arguments. This is largely driven by Futhark’s compiler implementing parametric polymorphism through monomorphisation, which does not traditionally mesh well with polymorphic recursion (although some forms can be handled).

Yet complete monomorphic recursion turned out to interact poorly with size types. Consider this reasonable function for summing arrays whose size is a power of two:

def sum [n] (xs: [n]i32) =
  if n == 1 then xs[0]
  else sum (map2 (+) (take (n/2) xs)
                     (take (n/2) (drop (n/2) xs)))

Technically, this is polymorphic recursion: we are defining the function for an input of type [n]i32, and the recursive call is with an argument of type [n/2]i32. However, monomorphisation does not take specific sizes into account, so there is no reason to rule out this definition. Hence, Futhark allows size-polymorphic recursion, but still not polymorphism in type parameters.

As a minor detail, Futhark programs are type checked in strict top-to-bottom order, and for this reason we do not allow mutual recursion. There is no deep reason why not. In fact, the main obstacle is that we would need to come up with a syntax for indicating that two functions are part of the same “binding group”, or whatever we end up calling it.

Higher-order recursive functions

The most subtle problem we had to address turned out to involve defunctionalisation. As a reminder to those readers who do not maintain encyclopedic mental notes of Futhark implementation details, Futhark implements higher-order functions via defunctionalisation, where any use of a higher-order function is turned into a first-order function by specialising at compile-time based on the higher-order arguments provided. As an example, if we have

def apply (f: i32 -> i32) (x: i32) = f x

then an application f (\x -> x + 1) 2 will result in a specialised function

def apply_specialised (x: i32) = (\x -> x + 1) x

and the original call will be rewritten to apply_specialised 2. There’s a little more to it than this, since the higher-order functions may be closures, so the specialised functions have parameters corresponding to captured environments - see our paper for details. That does not matter for the problem I would like to discuss, however. Consider a recursive higher-order function like this:

def naughty (f: i32 -> i32) (x: i32) =
  if x == 0 then f 42 else naughty (\y -> f y + 1) (x-1)

This function contains a recursive call to itself, but the higher-order parameter f is passed an a new function that captures the old function in every recursive call. If we imagine what this might look like when evaluated in a normal functional language, we can think of a linked list of closures, with each f linking to the previous one. From a Futhark perspective, this is already something that raises suspicion, since even though we add recursive functions, we still do not want recursive data. But the real problem is actually that the “shape” of the function passed to naughty cannot be known statically, since it depends on the depth of the recursion, which is controlled by the dynamic value x. Any attempt to defunctionalise naughty results in an infinite number of specialisations, and indeed, that is what happened.

The simplest solution to this problem is to not allow recursive higher-order functions at all, meaning they do not have to be defunctionalised at all. I do not actually have any compelling examples of recursive higher-order Futhark functions at hand, but it still felt a bit too restrictive. After all, the coolest part of creating a programming language is when people use it to write programs you had not thought of. Hence we impose a slightly simpler restriction: in a function, any recursive call must be provided arguments for all of its higher-order parameters, and they must be syntactically identical to the corresponding parameter in the definition. Intuitively it means you need to pass the same functions in the recursive call as were passed to you. This bans naughty above, and means that when generating a specialised version of a higher-order function, we can assume that any occurrence of that function in its own body will refer to the same specialisation, neatly tying the knot. This rule will not work with mutually recursive functions, but we’ll cross that bridge if we ever get to it.

Although a bit ad-hoc (syntactic checks?!), it is at least a simple rule, and I greatly prefer slightly inflexible rules to subtle but more flexible rules, and surely the inability to handle mutual recursion will not be a problem.

Lambda lifting can introduce mutual recursion

Apart from monomorphisation and defunctionalisation (and many other things), the Futhark compilation pipeline also performs lambda lifting. This is a program transformation where any lambdas are turned into named top level functions. The purpose is to simplify subsequent compiler passes and code generation. As an example, consider this contrived version of fact, where we add a useless lambda:

def fact_lam (n: i64) =
  if n == 0 then 1 else (\n' -> fact_lam n' * n) (n-1)

Applying lambda lifting to this program will result in this, where lifted_lam corresponds to the lifted lambda:

def lifted_lam (n: i64) (n': i64) =
  fact_lam' n' * n

def fact_lam' (n: i64) =
  if n == 0 then 1 else lifted_lam (n-1)

Now we have a problem: fact_lam' calls lifted_lam, and lifted_lam calls fact_lam'. These functions are mutually recursive. However, it turns out not to be a real problem, as lambda lifting a function that obeys the restrictions on recursive higher order functions does not produce the “infinitely growing” cases that can loop defunctionalisation. Hence, as long as we ensure that the various compiler passes downstream of lambda lifting can handle mutual recursion, we will be fine. It did take me by surprise for a minute, though.

That’s it

This is what it took to implement recursive functions. Fortunately, the code generator was already able to deal with recursive functions in CPU code, largely because it tends to just work in a straightforward implementation. Now, I should re-emphasize that the big hammer for handling recursion, flattening, will often produce dreadful code. We really need to look into which special patterns can be recognised and handled more efficiently. I also found through my (very sparse) experiments that writing recursive data parallel code can quickly consume a lot of memory, since your “Stack frames” end up containing large arrays that are memory-managed as monoliths, in contrast to classic functional languages that allow for more fine-grained liveness tracking. I am slightly worried that future Futhark programmers will tend to reach for recursion even in cases where it is not the best tool for the job.

As of this writing, recursion is not enabled in Futhark’s master branch (nor in any release), but the pull request that adds recursive functions merely removes the check that disables it, so all of the supporting code is already merged and active. It is also possible to experimentally allow recursion by setting a secret environment variable appropriately, although if any users want to experiment, it is best to do that on the branch that implements flattening (or just wait for it to be merged, which will probably be soon).

I still have not said much about how to actually use recursion to write potentially interesting programs. That will have to wait for the next post, because it turns out that to exploit the full power of data-parallel recursive programming, we need to add a new programming construct that more directly exposes flattening to the user.

blocks.html_en: It is not difficult to imagine a rule that says “you can have recursive functions, but not in code that ends up running on a GPU”. I do not actually have any compelling examples of recursive higher-order Futhark functions at hand, but it still felt a bit too restrictive. After all, the coolest part of creating a programming language is when people use it to write programs you had not thought of. Hence we impose a slightly simpler restriction: in a function, any recursive call must be provided arguments for all of its higher-order parameters, and they must be syntactically identical to the corresponding parameter in the definition. Intuitively it means you need to pass the same functions in the recursive call as were passed to you. content_html_zh:
发表于 2026 年 8 月 5 日

Futhark 在函数式语言中很不寻常，因为它目前不支持递归函数。 这并不是因为我们认为递归本质上是不好的——Futhark 编译器本身包含大量的递归定义。 原因是直到最近，我们还没有一个很好的答案来解决如何在每个后端的所有位置编译递归函数，而在 Futhark 中，我们更愿意只做出我们能够遵守的承诺。 这篇文章将解释为什么递归对于 Futhark 的存在来说一直是一个敏感的话题，为什么我们认为我们终于可以解决它，当我认为它很容易时出现了一些意想不到的麻烦，以及为什么 Futhark 程序员仍然可能不想过多使用它。

我考虑将这篇博文命名为“恢复 Futhark 的递归”，因为从技术上讲，Futhark 最早的草案确实支持递归函数，直到 2017 年被删除。 这意味着在 Futhark 一生的大部分时间里，特别是在 Futhark 发展成为一种具有模块、高阶函数和大小类型等功能的适当可用语言的时代。 此外，它们从来没有工作得那么好，如果你在错误的地方使用递归，编译器就会崩溃。

递归的麻烦

我们目前没有递归函数的原因相当简单：由于多种原因，它们在 GPU 内核中不能很好地工作。 最直接的一个问题是 GPU 线程必然具有微小的堆栈。 另一个原因是，从 GPU 代码内分配内存也是不切实际的（或缓慢或不可能），这意味着所有内存都必须提前预先分配 - 当您有递归函数时，这很困难，其中总内存需求取决于动态控制流决策。 普通顺序循环更简单，因为一旦完成循环迭代，您就永远不会返回到它 - 但对于（非尾部）递归函数，您必须在无限的时间内保持激活记录完整。

不难想象这样一条规则：“你可以有递归函数，但不能在最终在 GPU 上运行的代码中使用”。 更困难的是精确地规定这样一个规则。 Futhark 不是一种“GPU 语言”，而是一种与硬件无关的数据并行语言，我们不想使类型系统复杂化来跟踪函数是否包含递归。 Futhark 有多个针对 CPU 的编译器后端，对于这些递归来说，实现起来很简单，但是为 GPU 编译程序的可能性意味着语言限制由所有支持的编译器目标的限制的并集组成。

这是因为我自己研究的首要梦想是，如果你有一个函数 f，那么我希望能够将该函数 f 有效地映射到集合 xs 上，无论集合 xs 的大小、f 可能做什么，或者它在什么机器上运行。 由于人们不断想出新机器和新FS，我可能会把我的整个职业生涯都花在这上面，但我离题了。 我的观点是，我不会满足于复杂或缺乏正交性的解决方案，并且我不想要无法映射的函数。

事实证明，对于像 Futhark 这样的函数式数组语言来说，缺乏递归并不是什么大问题。 由于核心数据类型（数组）不是归纳的，因此没有太多需要递归的内容，并且 Futhark 提供了循环语法来表达某些类型的尾递归（尽管出于前面解释的原因，我们不打算支持实际的尾调用优化）。

尽管如此，在某些情况下，递归是解决问题的自然方法，主要是递归分而治之。 并行算法库中的许多算法在 Futhark 中表达起来非常困难，并且需要手动转换和展平（但完成后运行速度相当快）。 如果我们能够编写像 Guy Blelloch 在 NESL 中所做的那样好的代码，那就太好了。

通过展平处理递归

有许多特殊的递归情况可以通过各种有效的方式处理（尾递归就是其中之一），但在我们实现这一点之前，我们需要一个适用于所有情况的通用解决方案，即使该通用解决方案将来只是一个后备解决方案。 我们的通用解决方案（记住，只有在使用 GPU 后端时才需要）来自扁平化。 当展平表达式映射 f xs（其中 f 包含递归）时，递归实际上与映射“互换”，这意味着递归最终位于所有并行代码部分之外。 从操作角度来看，扁平化后所有递归控制流都在CPU上执行，而GPU则执行完全扁平化的并行操作。 为了直观地了解扁平化在这种情况下的工作原理，假设我们有递归函数式编程的 hello world：

def fact n = if n == 0 then 1 else n * fact (n-1)

现在假设我们将此函数映射到整数数组上：

map fact ns

显然这不是一件有用的事情，但它只是一个简单的例子。 在各种样板文件中，展平将产生事实的提升形式，它与原始事实一样递归，但对数组 ns 而不是单个 n 进行操作。 这个提升函数模拟递归的“单次迭代”，然后对 ns 中尚未达到其基本情况的元素执行递归调用。 简化记账和符号并添加解释性名称，它看起来像这样：

def fact_lifted ns =
  let (ns_zero, ns_nonzero) = partition_inputs ns
  let ns_nonzero' = map2 (*) ns_nonzero (fact_lifted ns_nonzero)
  let result = combine_inputs (map (const 1) ns_zero) ns_nonzero'
  in result

就像在扁平化帖子中一样，我主要是在挥手组合 mix_inputs 如何设法将事物按正确的顺序组合在一起。 关键属性是fact_lifted 只能从CPU 调用。 当然，虽然这种方法有效，但在许多情况下速度非常慢——partition_inputs和combine_inputs都隐藏了大量数据移动，但在短期内，我们关心的只是一般正确性——性能可以稍后实现。

我认为一旦我们实现了完全扁平化，递归就会很容易添加。 当然，编译器九年的密集开发意味着许多部分采用非递归程序，因此必须进行修复。 这些变化大部分都不是很有趣，但有一些发现是我没有预料到的。

在类型检查器中处理递归

Futhark 的类型检查器最近被大部分重写，对递归的适当支持是动机的一部分。 由于我们的类型检查算法基本上是传统的 Hindley-Milner，所以支持递归很简单，尽管我有一段时间意识到我实际上不知道如何做到这一点，因为我所有的 Hindley-Milner 实现经验都是针对非递归语言的。

与标准 ML 类似，但与 Haskell 不同，Futhark 不支持多态递归 - 任何递归调用都必须使用相同类型参数实例化递归函数。 这很大程度上是由 Futhark 的编译器通过单态化实现参数多态性驱动的，传统上它与多态递归不能很好地配合（尽管可以处理某些形式）。

然而，完整的单态递归与大小类型的交互效果很差。 考虑这个合理的函数来对大小为 2 的幂的数组求和：

def sum [n] (xs: [n]i32) =
  if n == 1 then xs[0]
  else sum (map2 (+) (take (n/2) xs)
                     (take (n/2) (drop (n/2) xs)))

从技术上讲，这是多态递归：我们为 [n]i32 类型的输入定义函数，并且递归调用使用 [n/2]i32 类型的参数。 然而，单态化没有考虑特定的大小，因此没有理由排除这个定义。 因此，Futhark 允许大小多态递归，但仍然不允许类型参数的多态性。

作为一个小细节，Futhark 程序按照严格的从上到下的顺序进行类型检查，因此我们不允许相互递归。 没有什么深层次的理由不这样做。 事实上，主要的障碍是我们需要想出一种语法来指示两个函数是同一个“绑定组”的一部分，或者无论我们最终如何称呼它。

高阶递归函数

事实证明，我们必须解决的最微妙的问题涉及去功能化。 提醒那些不记得 Futhark 实现细节的读者，Futhark 通过去功能化实现高阶函数，其中任何高阶函数的使用都会根据提供的高阶参数在编译时进行专门化，从而转换为一阶函数。 举个例子，如果我们有

def apply (f: i32 -> i32) (x: i32) = f x

那么应用 f (\x -> x + 1) 2 将产生一个专门的函数

def apply_specialised (x: i32) = (\x -> x + 1) x

原始调用将被重写为 apply_specialized 2。 还有比这更多的事情，因为高阶函数可能是闭包，所以专用函数具有与捕获的环境相对应的参数 - 有关详细信息，请参阅我们的论文。 不过，这对于我想讨论的问题来说并不重要。 考虑这样的递归高阶函数：

def naughty (f: i32 -> i32) (x: i32) =
  if x == 0 then f 42 else naughty (\y -> f y + 1) (x-1)

该函数包含对其自身的递归调用，但高阶参数 f 被传递给一个新函数，该新函数在每次递归调用中捕获旧函数。 如果我们想象一下用普通函数语言计算时会是什么样子，我们可以想到一个闭包链表，每个 f 都链接到前一个。 从 Futhark 的角度来看，这已经引起了怀疑，因为即使我们添加了递归函数，我们仍然不需要递归数据。 但真正的问题实际上是传递给 naughty 的函数的“形状”无法静态地知道，因为它取决于递归的深度，而递归的深度由动态值 x 控制。 任何使淘气功能化的尝试都会导致无数的专业化，事实上，这就是发生的事情。

这个问题最简单的解决方案是根本不允许递归高阶函数，这意味着它们根本不必被去功能化。 实际上，我手头没有任何令人信服的递归高阶 Futhark 函数的示例，但它仍然感觉有点过于严格。 毕竟，创建编程语言最酷的部分是当人们用它来编写你没有想到的程序时。 因此，我们施加了一个稍微简单的限制：在函数中，任何递归调用都必须为其所有高阶参数提供实参，并且它们在语法上必须与定义中相应的参数相同。 直观上，这意味着您需要在递归调用中传递与传递给您的函数相同的函数。 这禁止了上面的顽皮行为，并且意味着当生成高阶函数的专门版本时，我们可以假设该函数在其自身体内的任何出现都将引用相同的专门化，从而巧妙地结合在一起。 该规则不适用于相互递归函数，但如果我们到达它，我们就会跨过那座桥。

虽然有点临时（语法检查？！），但它至少是一个简单的规则，而且我非常喜欢稍微不灵活的规则，而不是微妙但更灵活的规则，并且肯定无法处理相互递归不会成为问题。

Lambda提升可以引入相互递归

除了单态化和去功能化（以及许多其他事情）之外，Futhark 编译管道还执行 lambda 提升。 这是一种程序转换，其中任何 lambda 都将转换为命名的顶级函数。 目的是简化后续编译器传递和代码生成。 举个例子，考虑这个人为设计的事实版本，其中我们添加了一个无用的 lambda：

def fact_lam (n: i64) =
  if n == 0 then 1 else (\n' -> fact_lam n' * n) (n-1)

将 lambda 提升应用于此程序将导致以下结果，其中 lift_lam 对应于提升的 lambda：

def lifted_lam (n: i64) (n': i64) =
  fact_lam' n' * n

def fact_lam' (n: i64) =
  if n == 0 then 1 else lifted_lam (n-1)

现在我们有一个问题：fact_lam'调用lifted_lam，lifted_lam调用fact_lam'。 这些函数是相互递归的。 然而，事实证明这并不是一个真正的问题，因为 lambda 提升一个遵守递归高阶函数限制的函数不会产生可以循环去功能化的“无限增长”情况。 因此，只要我们确保 lambda 提升下游的各个编译器传递可以处理相互递归，就可以了。 不过，这确实让我惊讶了一分钟。

这就是实现递归函数所需要的。 幸运的是，代码生成器已经能够处理 CPU 代码中的递归函数，这主要是因为它往往只在简单的实现中工作。 现在，我应该再次强调，处理递归、扁平化的大锤常常会产生可怕的代码。 我们确实需要研究哪些特殊模式可以被更有效地识别和处理。 我还通过我的（非常稀疏的）实验发现，编写递归数据并行代码会快速消耗大量内存，因为您的“堆栈帧”最终包含作为整体进行内存管理的大型数组，这与允许更细粒度的活动跟踪的经典函数语言形成鲜明对比。 我有点担心未来的 Futhark 程序员会倾向于使用递归，即使它不是工作的最佳工具。

截至撰写本文时，Futhark 的主分支（也没有在任何版本中）尚未启用递归，但添加递归函数的拉取请求只是删除了禁用它的检查，因此所有支持代码都已合并并处于活动状态。 还可以通过适当设置秘密环境变量来实验性地允许递归，尽管如果任何用户想要进行实验，最好在实现扁平化的分支上进行（或者只是等待它被合并，这可能很快）。

关于如何实际使用递归来编写可能有趣的程序，我还没有说太多。 这将不得不等待下一篇文章，因为事实证明，为了充分利用数据并行递归编程的全部功能，我们需要添加一个新的编程结构，更直接地向用户公开扁平化。
